title: Mild Brain Injury and ICT
subtitle: A four-study doctoral programme in consumer health informatics

slides.title: Mild Brain Injury and ICT
slides.standfirst: Four phases exploring how people with mild acquired cognitive impairment use and experience everyday technology — and, simultaneously, whether user experience research methods work with this population at all.

bullets.text: Principal Researcher, Doctoral Candidate
JMIR, PLOS ONE ×2, and the thesis
To the authors' knowledge, the first studies of ICT and user experience for health information consumers with MACI

slides.notes: Seven years of work. Present it as four questions in sequence, never as four papers — the sequence is the contribution.

slides.title: Mild acquired cognitive impairment
slides.standfirst: A minor, non-progressive decrease in cognitive function acquired through physical trauma or medical conditions — benign tumour, stroke, treatment side effects.
slides.notes: Define MACI properly before anything else. Most audiences will substitute dementia, which is almost the opposite: progressive, older, and well studied.

slides.title: Young, stabilising, and absent from the literature

bullets.text: Generally young — this is not an ageing cohort.
Expected to reach a stable cognitive level over time, not to decline.
Largely absent from health informatics research.
Tools designed for progressive impairment fit badly, and tools designed for the general population assume capacities that fluctuate here.

items.alt: Everyday information and communication technology in use
items.label: Everyday ICT, the object of study

items.alt: The four-phase research programme, as a wheel
items.label: The programme

slides.notes: Stable and young matters commercially as well as clinically: these are people with decades of technology use ahead of them.

slides.title: Two gaps, compounding each other

bullets.text: Almost no evidence about what ICT tools had been built or evaluated for self-management in this group, and no clear direction on how to proceed.
Capturing the user experience of people with cognitive impairment is itself methodologically unsolved.

callout.text: The standard UX field study toolkit assumes recall, sustained attention and self-report accuracy that cannot be taken for granted here. So studying the population and studying how to study the population had to happen simultaneously.

slides.notes: This is the intellectual spine of the whole programme. If the audience only remembers one slide, make it this one.

slides.title: Four phases, each answering the question the previous one raised

items.label: I · Systematic review
items.detail: What exists? 8 databases, 55 search phrases, ICF-derived analytical framework

items.label: II · National survey
items.detail: What do people actually use? 282 participants, purpose-built instrument, CFQ

items.label: III · Network analysis
items.detail: How do they communicate? A full year of a 1,310-member Facebook community

items.label: IV · Diary field study
items.detail: Can we study them at all? Day Reconstruction Method with 11 participants

figure.caption: Not four papers — one argument in four moves

callout.text: The review found interpersonal interaction unmet, which is why phase III studies communication. And because capturing the experience of this population is itself unsolved, phase IV interrogates the method rather than the population.

slides.notes: Point out the causal chain out loud: the review found interpersonal interaction unmet, which is why phase III is about communication.

slides.title: How empty was the evidence base?
slides.notes: Set this up as a genuine question. The answer is more extreme than anyone expects.

slides.title: Five thousand nine hundred and sixty-nine articles. Seven qualified.

figure.caption: A near-empty evidence base, established rather than asserted

slides.notes: Let the number land before speaking. Seven out of 5,969 is the justification for the entire doctoral programme existing.

slides.title: The framework was built, not borrowed
slides.standfirst: Tool functionality was analysed against an analytical framework derived from a subset of the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, cross-validated with Swedish MACI experts.

bullets.text: So functionality mapped to recognised domains of functioning rather than to feature names.
Swedish MACI clinicians checked the subset before it was used.
Specific unmet needs identified — notably support for interpersonal interactions and relationships.

slides.notes: Interpersonal interaction is the finding that steers the rest of the programme. Flag it explicitly here so phase III does not look like a change of subject.

slides.title: So what do people with MACI actually use?
slides.notes: Transition: the review said the literature is empty. Phase II goes and asks the population directly.

slides.title: A purpose-designed survey, paired with a validated cognitive measure
slides.standfirst: No existing instrument fit, so one was built — and deliberately coupled to the Cognitive Failure Questionnaire so results could be interpreted against impairment level rather than in the abstract.

bullets.text: Purpose-designed rather than adapted.
A validated measure of everyday cognitive failure, administered alongside.
Expert advisory committee, then pilot testing.
Calculated for a finite population of 1,300 persons.
Confirmatory and exploratory factor analysis, descriptive and percentile statistics.

figure.caption: 282 persons with acquired brain injury participated

slides.notes: Pairing the questionnaire with the CFQ is the methodological move worth explaining. It turns "people with brain injury" into a graded variable.

figure.caption: A graded measure, not a binary diagnosis

slides.notes: The standard deviation of 18 is as informative as the mean. This is a wide-spread population, which is precisely why a single design cannot serve it.

slides.title: E-service use is comparable to the healthy population. Facebook use is not.

figure.caption: 89% on e-services, 26% on Facebook against 71% nationally

slides.notes: This is the single most useful finding in the programme. Capability is not the barrier — 89% manage e-services. Something specific about social platforms is.

slides.title: "An external brain"
slides.standfirst: Content analysis of open-ended responses produced categories that describe technology as prosthesis rather than as convenience.

slides.title: If interpersonal interaction is the unmet need, what does it look like unobserved?
slides.notes: Emphasise unobserved. The whole design of phase III follows from not wanting to ask people to report on their own communication.

slides.title: Non-obtrusive, because asking would have changed the answer
slides.standfirst: A full year of a public Facebook group for Swedish speakers with brain fatigue, analysed without intervening — graph theory for the structure, directed qualitative content analysis for the meaning.

bullets.text: A 1,310-member public community.
1,092 unique active members — 83% of the group.
A full calendar year.
Graph-theoretic quantitative analysis plus directed qualitative content analysis.

slides.notes: 83% active participation in an online health community is remarkably high. Most such groups run on a small fraction of their membership.

slides.title: Contribution has a shape
slides.notes: The ladder from liking to commenting to posting is a cost ladder. In a fatigue population, that cost is cognitive, not social.

slides.title: The community gives more support than it asks for
slides.standfirst: Posts predominantly provided support rather than sought it — and informational support was the dominant content type.

figure.caption: Providing outweighed seeking by more than two to one

slides.notes: This inverts the usual assumption about patient communities as help-seeking spaces. It also implies the network is dense even without highly active nodes.

slides.title: The network, four ways

figure.caption: Graph-theoretic analysis of a full year

slides.notes: The dense graph without dominant hubs is the visual finding. Point at it rather than describing centrality measures.

slides.title: Does the UX field study toolkit work here at all?
slides.notes: The methodological question, finally asked head on. This phase exists to answer the second of the two original gaps.

slides.title: The Day Reconstruction Method was chosen for what it does not do
slides.standfirst: It does not interrupt daily activity, and it takes less time than other experience sampling methods — both of which matter enormously in a fatigue population.

bullets.text: 11 participants from 88 invited.
Daily activities across 17 activity categories.
Rated on a 0 to 6 Likert scale.
Time spent, and computer and Internet use.

slides.notes: 11 from 88 is a recruitment reality worth naming. It is not a weakness of the study; it is a fact about the population that anyone designing for it needs to know.

slides.notes: Do not narrate seven charts. Scroll once, say what the axes are, and move on to the methodological conclusion.

slides.title: With no data on non-participants, these are indications, not distributions
slides.standfirst: Every finding in the programme was framed as a rough population-level indication rather than as a distribution claim.

callout.text: A study of a hard-to-reach population that claims representativeness is claiming something it cannot have. Stating the limit is what makes the rest usable.

slides.notes: Include this slide even under time pressure. It is the difference between research and a report.

slides.title: Every instrument was selected for feasibility before findings

cards.title: Build the instrument
cards.text: A new ICF-based questionnaire rather than an adapted one, because nothing existing was designed for this population's capacities.

cards.title: Pair it with a cognitive measure
cards.text: The CFQ alongside, so results could be interpreted against impairment level instead of treating the cohort as homogeneous.

cards.title: Observe, don't ask
cards.text: Non-obtrusive social network analysis, so communication behaviour could be studied without relying on self-report.

cards.title: Choose the lightest diary
cards.text: DRM specifically because it does not interrupt activity and costs less participant time than other experience sampling.

slides.notes: This slide is the transferable content. Anyone researching a cognitively impaired, fatigued or otherwise burdened population can use all four.

slides.notes: Read 5,969 → 7 and 89% versus 26%. Those two pairs carry the whole programme.

slides.title: When you cannot trust your instruments, the method becomes the research
slides.standfirst: The temptation with an under-studied population is to run the standard playbook and publish whatever comes out. This programme treated instrument feasibility as a first-class research question — and that is why the findings stand.

callout.text: 89% e-service use against 26% Facebook use says capability is not the barrier. Something about the design of social platforms is. That is a design brief, produced by research that took the trouble to be trustworthy first.

slides.notes: End on the design brief. It connects seven years of academic work to something a product team could act on tomorrow.
